   128→["Kinematics","Physics","For constant acceleration: v=u+at, s=ut+½at², v²=u²+2as.",[Q("u=0, a=2 m/s², t=3 s. v = ?",["3 m/s","6 m/s","9 m/s"],1,"v = 0 + 2×3 = 6."),Q("Area under a v–t graph gives",["Acceleration","Displacement","Force"],1,"∫v dt is displacement.")]],
   129→["Newton’s laws","Physics","F = ma. Action–reaction pairs act on different bodies.",[Q("5 kg, net force 20 N. a = ?",["4 m/s²","100 m/s²","0.25 m/s²"],0,"a = F/m."),Q("Action and reaction act on",["The same body","Different bodies","Neither"],1,"So they never cancel each other.")]],
   130→["Work and energy","Physics","W = Fd cosθ, KE = ½mv². Net work equals the change in KE.",[Q("KE of 2 kg at 3 m/s",["9 J","6 J","18 J"],0,"½×2×9 = 9 J."),Q("Work by a force ⟂ displacement",["Maximum","Zero","Negative"],1,"cos 90° = 0.")]],
   131→["Units and measurements","Physics (Lumio-written practice, not official)","A physical quantity is something we can measure, and a measurement is a number together with a unit. The SI system has seven base quantities: length (metre), mass (kilogram), time (second), electric current (ampere), temperature (kelvin), amount of substance (mole) and luminous intensity (candela). Every other unit is derived from these, so force is kg m s⁻² (the newton). The dimensions of a quantity show how it depends on the base quantities, for example work and energy have dimensions [M L² T⁻²]. A dimensional check can show that an equation is wrong, but it cannot prove an equation is right, because pure numbers and constants like ½ have no dimensions. Only quantities with the same dimensions can be added or subtracted. Significant figures show how precise a measurement is: non-zero digits always count, zeros between digits count, leading zeros do not, and trailing zeros after a decimal point do. Percentage error is (absolute error ÷ measured value) × 100. A common mistake is to treat dimensional agreement as proof that a formula is correct.",[Q("Base-unit form of the newton (SI unit of force)",["kg m s⁻²","kg m² s⁻²","kg m s⁻¹"],0,"F = ma, so the unit is kg × m/s²."),Q("Dimensions of work and energy",["[M L T⁻²]","[M L² T⁻²]","[M L² T⁻¹]"],1,"Work = force × distance = [M L T⁻²] × [L]."),Q("Significant figures in 0.00450",["2","3","5"],1,"Leading zeros do not count. The 4, 5 and the trailing 0 after the decimal point do."),Q("Which quantity has the same dimensions as work?",["Torque","Power","Momentum"],0,"Torque = force × distance, so it is [M L² T⁻²]. Power is that divided by time."),Q("L = 12.0 cm with an absolute error of 0.1 cm. Percentage error ≈",["0.83%","1.2%","0.1%"],0,"0.1 ÷ 12.0 × 100 ≈ 0.83%."),Q("A dimensional check on a formula can show it is…",["Definitely correct","Possibly correct but not proven","Always wrong"],1,"It only tests dimensions. Numerical factors and missing terms go unnoticed.")]],
   132→["Motion in a straight line","Physics (Lumio-written practice, not official)","Distance is the total path length and is never negative, while displacement is the change in position and can be positive, negative or zero. Average velocity is displacement divided by time, and average speed is distance divided by time. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. For constant acceleration along a straight line: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² and v² = u² + 2as, where u is the initial velocity, v the final velocity and s the displacement. The slope of a position–time graph gives velocity, the slope of a velocity–time graph gives acceleration, and the area under a velocity–time graph gives displacement. A body dropped near the Earth’s surface falls with acceleration g, about 9.8 m/s² downward, if air resistance is ignored. A common mistake is to use the constant-acceleration equations when the acceleration is changing, or to forget the sign of a quantity when it points in the negative direction.",[Q("A body moves 5 m forward then 2 m back along a line. Displacement and distance are",["3 m and 7 m","7 m and 3 m","3 m and 3 m"],0,"Displacement = 5 − 2 = 3 m. Distance = 5 + 2 = 7 m."),Q("u = 10 m/s, a = −2 m/s², t = 3 s. v = ?",["16 m/s","4 m/s","−4 m/s"],1,"v = 10 + (−2)(3) = 4 m/s."),Q("u = 0, a = 4 m/s², t = 3 s. s = ?",["12 m","18 m","36 m"],1,"s = ½ × 4 × 3² = 18 m."),Q("u = 0 and v = 20 m/s over s = 50 m. a = ?",["4 m/s²","8 m/s²","0.25 m/s²"],0,"a = v² ÷ 2s = 400 ÷ 100 = 4 m/s²."),Q("The slope of a position–time graph gives",["Acceleration","Velocity","Displacement"],1,"Slope = change in position ÷ change in time = velocity."),Q("Dropped from rest (take g = 10 m/s², no air resistance). Speed after 3 s = ?",["30 m/s","15 m/s","90 m/s"],0,"v = gt = 10 × 3 = 30 m/s.")]],
   133→["Gravitation","Physics (Lumio-written practice, not official)","Newton’s law of gravitation says every two masses attract each other with a force F = Gm₁m₂/r², where r is the distance between their centres and G is the gravitational constant. The force is always attractive and falls with the square of the distance. Near a planet of mass M and radius R, the acceleration due to gravity is g = GM/R². Gravitational potential energy is U = −GMm/r, which is negative and tends to zero at infinite distance. Escape speed from the surface is √(2GM/R), which is √2 times the orbital speed just above the surface. Kepler’s third law states that the square of a planet’s orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit. Astronauts in orbit feel weightless because they and the spacecraft are both in free fall, not because gravity has vanished. A common mistake is to measure r from the surface instead of from the centre of the planet.",[Q("If the distance between two masses doubles, the gravitational force becomes",["Half","One quarter","Double"],1,"F ∝ 1/r², so doubling r divides F by 4."),Q("A planet has the same mass as Earth but twice the radius. Its surface g is",["g/2","g/4","2g"],1,"g = GM/R², so doubling R divides g by 4."),Q("Escape speed compared with orbital speed just above the surface",["√2 times larger","Twice as large","Equal"],0,"v_escape = √2 × v_orbit."),Q("An orbit’s radius becomes 4 times larger. The period becomes",["4 times","8 times","16 times"],1,"T² ∝ r³, so T ∝ r^(3/2) = 4^(3/2) = 8."),Q("Astronauts in orbit feel weightless because",["Gravity is zero there","They and the spacecraft are in free fall","They are outside Earth’s gravitational field"],1,"Gravity at that height is still strong, about 90% of its surface value for a low orbit."),Q("As r → ∞ the gravitational potential energy U = −GMm/r tends to",["0","−∞","+∞"],0,"The magnitude GMm/r shrinks towards zero.")]],
   134→["Oscillations","Physics (Lumio-written practice, not official)","An oscillation repeats its motion about a mean position. In simple harmonic motion (SHM) the restoring force is proportional to the displacement and points towards the mean position, so x = A cos(ωt + φ), where A is the amplitude and ω = 2π/T is the angular frequency. The speed is greatest at the mean position, where it equals Aω, and zero at the extremes. The acceleration is greatest at the extremes, where it equals Aω², and zero at the mean position. A mass m on a spring of constant k has T = 2π√(m/k). A simple pendulum of length L swinging through small angles has T = 2π√(L/g), which does not depend on the mass. The total energy of SHM is ½kA² and stays constant while it swaps between kinetic and potential energy. A common mistake is to say the speed is greatest at the extremes: it is zero there.",[Q("A 1 kg mass on a spring with k = 100 N/m.    135→["Thermal properties of matter","Physics (Lumio-written practice, not official)","Temperature tells how hot something is, while heat is energy that flows because of a temperature difference. A change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K. The heat needed to change the temperature of a mass m is Q = mcΔT, where c is the specific heat capacity. Water has a high specific heat capacity, about 4200 J/(kg·K), which is why it heats and cools slowly. During a change of state, such as melting or boiling, the temperature stays constant and the heat supplied (latent heat, Q = mL) changes how the particles are arranged instead. Heat travels by conduction in solids, by convection in fluids and by radiation through empty space. A rod of length L heated by ΔT expands by ΔL = αLΔT, where α is the coefficient of linear expansion. A common mistake is to confuse heat with temperature: a large cup of warm water holds more heat than a spark that is much hotter.",[Q("How much heat raises 2 kg of water by 10 °C? (c = 4200 J/(kg·K))",["84 000 J","8400 J","840 000 J"],0,"Q = mcΔT = 2 × 4200 × 10 = 84 000 J."),Q("A temperature rise of 20 °C is the same as a rise of",["20 K","293 K","253 K"],0,"The size of one degree is the same on both scales, so the change is 20 K."),Q("While ice melts at 0 °C, the heat supplied goes into",["Raising the temperature","Changing the state (latent heat)","Nothing at all"],1,"The temperature stays constant during a change of state."),Q("A 2 m rod has α = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ per K and is heated by 50 K. Its length increases by",["1.2 mm","12 mm","0.12 mm"],0,"ΔL = αLΔT = 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ × 2 × 50 = 1.2 × 10⁻³ m = 1.2 mm.")]],
   136→["Python: functions and loops","Computer Science / Python (Lumio-written practice, not official)","A function is a named block of code that you define with the keyword def and call by name. It can take parameters and send a value back with return, so def double(x): return x * 2 gives double(4) equal to 8. A for loop repeats code for each item in a sequence, and range(n) produces the numbers 0 up to n − 1. A while loop repeats as long as its condition stays true, so it needs something inside that eventually makes the condition false. The operator // gives the whole-number part of a division and % gives the remainder, so 10 // 3 is 3 and 10 % 3 is 1. The built-in len() returns how many items a string or list holds. Indentation is part of Python’s syntax and shows which lines belong inside a function or loop. A common mistake is forgetting that range stops before its end value, or printing a value inside a function when the task asks you to return it. Practise these ideas in Practice & Games, then Coding Lab.",[Q("range(4) produces",["1, 2, 3, 4","0, 1, 2, 3","0, 1, 2, 3, 4"],1,"range starts at 0 and stops before 4."),Q("def f(x): return x * 2.    469→def _lumio(code,fn,tests):
   470→    ns={}

   472→        exec(code,ns)
   473→    except Exception as er:
   474→        return json.dumps({"err":type(er).__name__+": "+str(er)})
   475→    f=ns.get(fn)

   478→    D=lambda v:json.dumps(v,separators=(",",":"))

   480→    for a,x in json.loads(tests):
   481→        try:
   482→            g=f(*a)
   483→        except Exception as er:
   484→            g="error: "+type(er).__name__+": "+str(er)
   485→        try:
   486→            gj=D(g)
   487→        except Exception:
   488→            gj=repr(g)
   489→        out.append({"ok":gj==D(x),"t":fn+"("+", ".join(D(v) for v in a)+")","e":D(x),"g":gj})
   490→    return json.dumps({"res":out})`;
